newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-SACCHI WANTS TO BRING CRAMP TO MILAN'S STYLE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SACCHI WANTS TO BRING CRAMP TO MILAN'S STYLE.

text.p: New Year is generally a time to ring out the old and bring in the new. Going into 1997, AC Milan might happily settle for a repeat of the past.

The Italian champions can take little comfort from the present season after being beaten in the domestic cup, dismissed from European competition by Norwegians and with their serie A title hopes looking more and more the stuff of dreams.
The future is meanhile full of uncertainty.

For much of this season, the novelty for the once all-conquering Milan has been defeat and disorganisation on a rare scale while provincial soccer clubs such as Vicenza and Bologna impress with a fraction of their resources.
After capturing the serie A league title four times in the past five seasons and also winning the European Cup three times since 1988, Milan are looking lost and tired.
The "rosso-nere" (red-blacks) have lost five times in 14 league matches, compared with Juventus's sole defeat, despite the fact that only Vicenza have scored more goals.
This month's European Cup Champions' League defeat by Norway's Rosenborg proved that something was seriously wrong.
For the first time since media mogul Silvio Berlusconi took over as club president, Milan went out of the European Cup competition before the quarter-final stages.

Newly-appointed coach Arrigo Sacchi, who ironically represents the old rather than the new as the architect of Milan's success in the 1980s, faces a tough task in the months ahead as he seeks to rebuild the old spirit.
The New Year, with the opening match against Lazio in Rome on January 5, calls for a fresh approach.
"I want to see right from the first days of 1997 a more competitive Milan," Sacchi told reporters last week.
Hard work and determination are the key.

Sacchi, who took Italy to the 1994 World Cup final against Brazil, held up those players -- many of them coming from Milan -- as an example of what a less than outstanding team can achieve with the right psychological attitude.
"Many of those players left the pitch with cramp. They suffered and gave everything," he said.
"And, not by accident, we finished second. I would like to see Milan players leave the pitch with cramp also."
To that end Sacchi has re-introduced training methods abandoned by Tabarez, including midweek friendlies with local clubs, and made life much harder for the players.

A month on from the former Italian national coach's sensational return to the San Siro stadium following the resignation of courteous Uruguayan coach Oscar Washington Tabarez, the scale of the problem is clearer.
Milan are seventh, eight points adrift of leaders Juventus whose form is improving, and Sacchi publicly conceded at the weekend that Milan are fighting for second place.
His words may just be a ruse -- captain Franco Baresi angrily dismissed them by saying that he never plays for second place -- but they also smack of realism.
Sacchi's league record is not bad -- two wins and one defeat -- but Milan are far from convincing on the field.
Asked whether the current Milan players could emulate his 1988 title-winning team by fighting to the top after the Christmas break, Sacchi found no room for optimism.
"Absolutely no," the coach told Italian newspapers. "The conditions are not there. That team came after 10 years without success. This team has 10 years of success behind it."
Put simply, the coach believes that his team have become stale and spoilt by their success.
But injury has also taken its toll, with Liberian striker George Weah sidelined by an ankle problem and also banned from Europe for six matches for headbutting an opponent.

Italy defender Paolo Maldini, already wrestling with the worst season of his career, fractured a cheekbone in the last match against Parma before Christmas while former World Cup star Roberto Baggio has fallen out with Sacchi.
Other leading lights, such as 36-year-old Baresi, are already well into extra time in their careers.
"The team has a lot of problems, there is no point hiding it, said Sacchi last week, adding that it would be unfair to blame Tabarez or the athletic training of the players.
"We lack the right determination, we need to have patience, it will take time to find it," Sacchi warned.
He said several players, none named, were like shadows -- "present but absent" -- who made little effort.
"Before I came back to Milan, I thought that I would not find any (such players). I was evidently wrong."

Some new signings, with Dutchman Michael Reiziger a leading example, have made little impact and even Weah, world player of the year in 1995 and with a contract to the end of the century, has spoken openly about a possible move to English premier league club Arsenal.
Former Gothenburg midfielder Jesper Blomqvist, who joined Milan this month to instant acclaim, has meanwhile become firmly established at the club as a hope for the future.
He may be joined by Bayern Munich's Christian Ziege while Italian newspapers have reported that the club is chasing Ajax's Winston Bogarde and Patrick Kluivert for next season.
"For a club to recover, there are so many factors at work," Sacchi told the daily Gazzetta dello Sport newspaper.
"But two are fundamental: A club and a president who have faith and a group willing to make sacrifices.
It will be a hard year ahead.
